h1:
China Furniture Sourcing
Seating, Tables & Interior Pieces
lead: Furniture is the category where China is hardest to buy from without someone on the ground. Catalogues are huge, photographs are reused between factories, and the difference between a good batch and a bad one is usually in the frame, the foam and the finish — none of which show up in a listing. We buy furniture out of the Foshan and Shunde belt regularly, and we inspect it before it leaves.
sub_intro: These are the lines we quote most often in this category. If what you need sits between two of them, send the reference anyway — most first orders are mixed.

mat_intro: Most furniture disputes come down to a material that was described loosely. Naming the material, the finish and the standard up front is the cheapest quality control you can buy.

materials.name: Solid wood
materials.note: Oak, ash, walnut, rubberwood and beech. Ask for kiln-dried stock at 8–12% moisture content — anything wetter moves and cracks after it reaches a drier climate.

materials.name: Engineered board
materials.note: Plywood, MDF and particle board with veneer, melamine or lacquer. Cheaper and more dimensionally stable than solid wood; specify the formaldehyde class (E0, CARB or EPA) if your market requires it.

materials.name: Metal
materials.note: Steel, stainless steel and aluminium, powder-coated, brushed or plated. Check coating thickness and whether the frame is welded or bolted — it changes both strength and flat-pack feasibility.

materials.name: Rattan, cane & woven
materials.note: Natural rattan and cane webbing for interiors, PE rattan for outdoor. Natural material needs consistent grading, or colour drift shows across a container.

materials.name: Upholstery
materials.note: Polyester, linen blends and velvet fabrics, PU, and top-grain or split leather. Specify foam density, Martindale rub count and any fire-retardancy treatment your market requires.

materials.name: Stone & sintered surfaces
materials.note: Marble, granite, sintered stone and tempered glass for table tops and consoles. Heavy, fragile and usually worth crating rather than cartoning.

buy_intro: These are the numbers buyers ask for first. They are indicative ranges from recent orders, not a quotation — the real figures depend on the design, the finish and the factory slot.

buying.label: Typical MOQ
buying.note: Stocked designs usually start at one to ten pieces. Custom sizes, finishes or fabrics generally begin at ten to fifty units per model, because the factory has to set up a run.

buying.label: Lead time
buying.note: Seven to fifteen days for stocked items after the deposit; thirty to forty-five days for made-to-order. Everything slows down in the weeks before Chinese New Year.

buying.label: Sampling
buying.note: A finished sample is usually charged at one and a half to two times unit price plus courier, and is commonly credited back against the bulk order.

buying.label: Packaging
buying.note: Flat-pack in export cartons with corner protection as standard. Assembled pieces, and anything with stone or glass, are worth a wooden crate.

buying.label: Compliance
buying.note: EN 12520 and EN 12521 for strength and durability, BS 5852 or CA TB117 for fire retardancy, CARB or E0 for formaldehyde, FSC chain of custody on request.

buy_footnote: Treat these as the shape of a typical order, not a price list. We confirm the real figures with the factory before you commit to anything.
check_intro: The more of this you can send in the first message, the fewer rounds it takes to get to a number you can actually use.
checklist: Room dimensions, door widths and stair access — oversized sofas and beds fail at delivery more often than at the factory
Intended use: residential, rental, hospitality or commercial, because it changes foam density, frame joints and fabric rub count
Finish and colour reference — a Pantone, RAL code or physical swatch beats a photograph every time
Fabric or leather specification, including Martindale rub count and any fire-retardancy requirement
Packaging preference: flat-pack for freight efficiency, or assembled and crated for immediate use
Target landed cost per piece, so we can quote to a number instead of guessing what you can absorb
check_footnote: Send whatever you have — a screenshot, a dimensions sketch or a half-finished list. Missing pieces we can fill in together; wrong assumptions are what cost time.

compare.intro: Plenty of buyers can reach a furniture factory on their own. The difference shows up after the first quotation, when the specification starts to matter.

faq_intro: These are the questions that come up on almost every furniture brief.

faq.q: What is the minimum order for custom furniture?
faq.a: It is set by the factory, not by us. Stocked designs can often be bought one piece at a time, while a custom size, finish or fabric usually needs ten to fifty units per model because the factory has to set up a production run. We confirm the real number with each factory before you commit.

faq.q: Can you reproduce a design I saw somewhere else?
faq.a: Usually yes, if you can send photographs, dimensions and any detail shots of the joints and finish. We will tell you honestly where a design can be matched closely and where the original uses a process or material that is not worth reproducing at your volume.

faq.q: How much does it cost to ship furniture from China?
faq.a: Furniture is bulky, so freight is charged on volume rather than weight for most sea shipments. A consolidated part-container load is far cheaper per piece than a small standalone shipment. We quote freight on the actual packed volume after consolidation, not on an estimate made before the goods are packed.

faq.q: Do you handle hotel and project furniture?
faq.a: Yes. Hotel, villa and restaurant furniture is bought against a BOQ and a handover date rather than a single product link, and it goes through our B2B buying flow with factory shortlisting, sampling and pre-shipment inspection included.
